title: The Silk Road
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The Silk Road was not a single road. It was a network of trading routes that linked China with the Mediterranean for about fifteen hundred years. The name was invented in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, who wanted a simple way to describe the routes, and no traveller of the time ever used it. Very few merchants made the whole journey of more than six thousand kilometres. Instead, goods passed from trader to trader, and each one added a little to the price, so that a bolt of silk cost many times more in Rome than in China.

Silk was the most famous product, but it was far from the only one. Chinese craftsmen kept the method of making silk secret for centuries, and in Rome the cloth was worth almost its weight in gold. Caravans also carried spices, glass, horses, jade and paper. Travelling in the other direction, merchants brought gold, silver, wool and grapevines to China. The animal of choice was the camel, since a single camel could carry about two hundred kilograms and could go for days without water.

The journey was dangerous. Caravans crossed the Taklamakan Desert, whose name is often said to mean 'go in and you will not come out', and the high passes of the Pamir Mountains, where the air is thin and the cold can kill. Bandits were a constant threat. To protect themselves, merchants travelled in large groups and stayed overnight at caravanserais, walled inns built about a day's journey apart. A caravanserai offered water, food and a safe place for the animals, and its courtyard also served as a market where travellers could sell goods or exchange news.

Cities along the route grew rich. Samarkand, in what is now Uzbekistan, became one of the greatest trading centres in Central Asia, and its markets sold goods from three continents. Rulers taxed the merchants who passed through, and they spent the money on mosques, schools and observatories. The cities also became meeting places for languages and religions. Buddhism travelled from India to China along the same roads, and Islam later spread through Central Asia in the same way. A merchant in Samarkand might have spoken three or four languages.

Ideas moved as easily as goods. The art of papermaking reached the Arab world in the eighth century, after a battle near the River Talas in which Chinese prisoners taught their captors the craft. Paper later reached Europe and made printed books possible. Gunpowder, the compass and printing followed the same path westwards. Going east, mathematics from India and astronomy from the Islamic world influenced Chinese scholars, who were eager to learn from visitors.

Disease also travelled. Many historians believe that the Black Death, which killed a large share of the population of Europe in the fourteenth century, spread along trade routes from Central Asia. At about the same time, the Silk Road began to decline. The Mongol Empire, which had kept the routes safe for a century, broke up, and ships proved a cheaper way to move heavy cargo. By the sixteenth century, most merchants preferred the sea, and many of the caravanserais were abandoned.

Today the Silk Road is being rebuilt, in a way. China has paid for railways, roads and ports in many countries in a programme called the Belt and Road Initiative. Freight trains now carry goods between China and Europe in about two weeks, compared with around six weeks by sea. Supporters say that the projects bring jobs and trade to poorer countries. Critics reply that some governments are borrowing more than they can repay. Meanwhile, tourists follow the old route to see the mosques and markets of Samarkand and Bukhara.
